title: Per-tenant QoS profiles, soft-preemption windows, and bandwidth cages for GPU fleet isolation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
Implement a per-tenant Quality of Service (QoS) framework for the Dedicated GPU fleet that combines: (1) configurable QoS profiles (latency-first, throughput-first, cost-saver), (2) soft-preemption windows with graceful eviction semantics, and (3) per-tenant bandwidth cages (memory/PCIe and network bandwidth) to mitigate noisy neighbors. This ticket scopes the core runtime + scheduler changes, API surface for admins to assign QoS profiles, autoscaler policy hooks, and the rollout plan for an initial cohort of enterprise tenants.

Motivation / problem statement:
Customers on Dedicated often see performance variability caused by co-tenants bursting compute or IO (noisy neighbors). Current isolation is coarse (reservation pools + hard quotas) which either wastes capacity or leads to loud evictions. We need a middle ground that: minimizes tail latency regressions for latency-sensitive tenants, allows predictable throughput for reserved customers, and limits cost blowouts from greedy tenants.

Goals / acceptance criteria:
- Provide three default QoS profiles: latency-first, throughput-first, cost-saver. Admins can supply custom profiles via Console/API.
- Implement soft-preemption windows: when a tenant exceeds soft quota, requests are deprioritized and scheduled into a preemption-safe window (e.g., finish-in-flight tokens) instead of immediate termination.
- Enforce bandwidth cages per tenant for PCIe memory bandwidth and host-network egress to prevent IO saturation.
- Autoscaler integration: autoscaling policies can consult tenant QoS to decide between scaling capacity vs. applying throttles.
- Observable SLOs: per-tenant tail latency (p95/p99), throughput, and preemption events visible in Console with alerting thresholds.
- Rollout with canary tenants: no customer-facing downtime, opt-in initial cohort of 6 tenants, rollback plan tested in staging.

Design overview:
1) QoS profile model (control plane):
   - Stored as tenant metadata: profile name, soft_quota_tokens (tokens/min), hard_quota_tokens (tokens/min), preemption_window_ms, p99_target_ms, bandwidth_caps = {pcie_mb_s, net_mb_s}.
   - Admin API endpoints: POST/GET /tenants/{id}/qos-profile; Console UX to edit and preview estimated cost impact.

2) Runtime & scheduler changes (data plane):
   - Admission controller: checks current token usage; if over soft_quota but under hard_quota, mark request as "deprioritized" and attach a preemption-safe token. Requests with token are scheduled in slots reserved for deprioritized traffic.
   - Soft-preemption window enforcement: tasks in the window are allowed to complete a bounded number of micro-batches; runtime signals userland model runner to checkpoint KV cache and flush partial outputs on preemption.
   - Bandwidth cages: integrate with host-level cgroup-like egress shaping for network and use MIG/SM-level counters to estimate PCIe memory bandwidth; when cap is near, scheduler delays low-priority tasks.
   - Fallback routing: if tenant is throttled and latency-first profile requests are at risk, route to alternate lower-cost region or to a pre-warmed dedicated 'latency-shed' pool depending on policy.

3) Autoscaler hooks:
   - New autoscaler signals: tenant_qos_pressure (low/medium/high), preemption_rate, bandwidth_saturation. Policies can be written like: "scale when tenant_qos_pressure==high and preemption_rate>5% for 3m" or "apply throttle if scale budget exhausted".

4) Metrics and observability:
   - Emit per-tenant metrics: qos_profile, soft_quota_remaining, hard_quota_usage, preemption_events, p95_latency, p99_latency, pcie_bandwidth_usage, net_bandwidth_usage.
   - Console: new per-tenant QoS dashboard with historical charts and correlation links to traces and logs.

Trade-offs considered:
- Strict hardware isolation (dedicating N GPUs per tenant) -> best isolation but poor utilization and higher cost to customers. Not acceptable for multi-tenant Dedicated pools.
- Pure hard quotas and immediate kill on overage -> simple but causes noisy customer experience (request failures).
- Soft-preemption with deprioritization -> better UX but more complex: requires runtime hooks, consistent metrics, and careful testing to avoid starvation. We favor soft-preemption to balance UX and utilization.

Implementation plan (milestones):
- Week 1 (spike): validate PCIe and network bandwidth telemetry on representative fleet images; prototype preemption token in local scheduler (owner: Luca).
- Week 2: implement control-plane QoS profile schema + Admin API; Console draft for editing profiles (owner: PM).
- Week 3: integrate admission controller with deprioritized queues; add preemption-safe token flow into runtime (owner: runtime team).
- Week 4: implement bandwidth cages using host egress shaping and test regression scenarios; add autoscaler hooks.
- Week 5: staging canary rollout with 3 tenants; collect metrics, iterate on defaults.
- Week 6: expand to 6 tenants; document runbook and incidents.

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests for control-plane validation and API permissions.
- Integration test harness that simulates multi-tenant noisy IO and compute bursts; assert latency-first tenants meet p99 target within 2x baseline when mixed with aggressive tenants.
- Chaos testing: transient node loss while preemption windows active.
- Load test: synthetic traffic patterns to validate autoscaler signal correctness.

Rollout & migration plan:
- Initial opt-in: allow tenants to opt into new QoS profiles via Console; default behavior for existing tenants remains unchanged.
- Gradual enforcement: start with monitoring-only mode (emit events but do not deprioritize), then enable deprioritization only for opted-in tenants, and finally flip default for new Dedicated pools after 6 weeks.
- Revert: control-plane toggle to disable deprioritization and remove bandwidth cages per-region.

Open questions / risks:
- How accurate are PCIe bandwidth estimates on our existing NVIDIA stack? (spike needed).
- Interaction with existing reservation pools and burst reservations: need formal compatibility tests.
- Security: per-tenant shaping requires extra kernel capabilities — coordinate with infra security.

Links to artifacts and references:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.dev/display/INF/Per-Tenant+QoS+Profiles+Design (draft)
- Spike notes & telemetry queries: https://docs.redwood.dev/notes/qos-spike-2026-03
- Related PR (runtime admission): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4217 (WIP)
- Autoscaler policy examples: https://github.com/redwood-inference/autoscaler/tree/qos-hooks

Acceptance tests (explicit):
- Stage: opt-in tenant A (latency-first) + tenant B (throughput-first). Under a synthetic noisy-I/O burst from B, A's p99 latency increases by no more than 50% vs baseline and preemption events <2% after config tuning.
- Preemption tokens: ensure tasks with token can complete at least 2 micro-batches before eviction.
- Bandwidth cages: under sustained noisy neighbor egress, capped tenant's measured net_mb_s does not exceed the configured cap within +/-10%.

Deliverables:
- Control plane API and Console UX for QoS profiles.
- Runtime changes: admission controller, deprioritized queue, preemption-safe token behavior, bandwidth cage enforcement.
- Autoscaler integration and policy recipes.
- Documentation: runbook, user guide, rollback steps, and postmortem template.
